stem: A trained nurse who is authorized by the facility emergency plan to use a portable fire extinguisher sees a fire involving energized electrical equipment. Which extinguisher classification is appropriate for this hazard?
rationale: OSHA defines a Class C fire as one involving energized electrical equipment where electrically nonconductive extinguishing media are required for employee safety. Class A involves ordinary combustibles, Class B involves flammable or combustible liquids/gases and similar materials, and Class D involves combustible metals. The stem specifies energized electrical equipment and that the nurse is trained and authorized to use an extinguisher; some workplaces instead require evacuation by employees who are not designated extinguisher users. Therefore C is the best answer.
educational_objective: Recognize Class C fire-extinguisher classification for fires involving energized electrical equipment when the nurse is trained and authorized to use portable extinguishers.
source_organization: U.S. Department of Labor — Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
source_document_title: 29 CFR 1910.155 — Definitions Applicable to Fire Protection; OSHA Portable Fire Extinguisher eTool
source_locator: 29 CFR 1910.155(c)(8)-(11): definitions of Class A, B, C, and D fires; §1910.155(c)(10) defines Class C as a fire involving energized electrical equipment requiring electrically nonconductive extinguishing media. OSHA eTool 'Extinguisher Basics' likewise states energized electrical equipment requires an extinguisher labeled C
source_claim_supported: A fire involving energized electrical equipment is a Class C fire hazard under OSHA definitions.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Emergency Response Plan, printed p.25 / PDF p.29: use clinical decision-making/critical thinking for emergency response plan; participate in emergency planning and response
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — emergency response / fire extinguisher selection
correction_summary: Converted bare fire-class recall into a healthcare emergency scenario and explicitly specified energized electrical equipment. Added the condition that the nurse is trained and authorized to use an extinguisher, avoiding conflict with workplace emergency plans that require non-designated staff to evacuate rather than fight fires.
audit_findings: C directly matches OSHA's regulatory definition. A, B, and D are real fire classifications but correspond to different hazards, making them plausible and clearly incorrect here. The word 'energized' is necessary because after de-energization the remaining burning material may fall under another class. The authorized-user condition prevents a scope/safety second answer about evacuation. NCSBN 2026 maps the construct to emergency response. Independent second pass found one best answer and no unresolved conflict.

final_reaudit_scope: current OSHA fire classification/regulation; exact locator; claim-by-claim; A-D distractor audit; ambiguity/second-answer/cueing; NCSBN 2026 blueprint; independent adversarial second pass
